lesson.title: The Pressure That Keeps Plants Standing: Turgor Pressure
lesson.summary: Turgor pressure is the outward push of water-filled plant cells against their walls, and it is the main reason non-woody plants stay upright and stiff.
lesson.body:
Cut stems without wood, like a stalk of celery or a young sunflower seedling, still stand upright, and the explanation has nothing to do with rigid building material and everything to do with water pressure. Turgor pressure is the physical force that the contents of a plant cell exert outward against its cell wall as a result of water entering by osmosis. In the language of the previous section, turgor pressure is the pressure potential component of water potential made visible. When a plant cell sits in a solution with a higher water potential than the cell's interior, water follows its potential gradient and enters the cell, mostly filling the large central vacuole, which can occupy most of a mature plant cell's volume.

As water accumulates inside, the vacuole and cytoplasm swell and press the plasma membrane against the surrounding cell wall. Unlike an animal cell membrane, the cellulose cell wall does not stretch indefinitely, so it pushes back with an equal and opposite force called wall pressure. This standoff is not a failure of the system, it is the system working as intended. Water keeps entering only until the rising pressure potential inside the cell exactly balances the difference in solute potential between the cell and its surroundings, at which point total water potential is equal on both sides and net water movement stops. The cell has reached a stable, turgid state, firm and swollen, with positive turgor pressure sustained indefinitely as long as the external water supply holds.

This pressure does real mechanical work. In herbaceous plants and in the soft tissues of even woody plants, turgor pressure is the primary source of structural support, letting leaves stay outstretched and stems stay upright without needing the lignin-reinforced secondary walls found in wood. Guard cells surrounding each stomatal pore rely on the same mechanism at a much smaller scale: when guard cells take up water and become turgid, their uneven wall thickness forces them to bow outward, opening the stomatal pore for gas exchange, and when they lose turgor the pore closes. Turgor pressure is therefore not just a passive support mechanism, it is an actively regulated lever that plants use to control their own physiology minute by minute.

The consequences of losing turgor are equally visible. When a plant is placed in a hypertonic environment, such as soil laden with fertilizer salt or seawater flooding a coastal marsh, the external water potential drops below the water potential of the cell, and water leaves the cell by osmosis. As the vacuole shrinks, the protoplast pulls away from the rigid cell wall entirely, a condition called plasmolysis, and turgor pressure falls toward zero or even becomes slightly negative. A plant experiencing widespread plasmolysis in its tissues wilts, its leaves and stems drooping because the cells that once pushed against their walls no longer have the internal pressure to do so.

Watering a wilted plant reverses this process directly, illustrating how tightly turgor pressure is tied to the osmotic gradients described earlier: as soil water potential rises above the water potential inside the root and stem cells, water re-enters, vacuoles refill, and pressure potential climbs back toward its turgid equilibrium, often within hours. This everyday observation, a drooping plant perking back up after watering, is one of the clearest demonstrations available of how water potential, osmosis, and cell wall mechanics combine to produce a mechanical property with real consequences for how a plant survives.
